newsitem.title: USA: Judge rules for Time Warner in News Corp dispute.
newsitem.headline: Judge rules for Time Warner in News Corp dispute.

text.p: A federal judge Wednesday issued a preliminary injunction against New York City, preventing it from forcing Time Warner Inc to carry News Corp Ltd's new Fox News 24-hour cable television programming on channels devoted to New York City programming.

U.S. District Judge Denise Cote ruled that Time Warner had established that the city had violated Time Warner's rights under the federal Cable Act and under the First Amendment of the U.S. Constitution.
The order also prevents New York City from airing Bloomberg Information Television on city-run channels.

The dispute centers on the role of the city's five stations, known as Crosswalks. New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani decided to place the new 24-hour Fox programming on one of the Crosswalks channels after Time Warner had rejected it. He also planned to run Bloomberg's news programming on a station.

Time Warner, which serves 1.1 million cable TV customers in New York, sued the city, alleging that Giuliani was acting on behalf of Rupert Murdoch's News Corp, which owns the New York Post and WNYW-TV. It alleged in its suit that the city was acting as Murdoch's "latest political puppet."

"This case concerns the power of a city to influence, control and even coerce the programming decision of an operator of a cable television system. It therefore goes to the heart of First Amendment concerns," Cote wrote in her 106 page ruling.

Cote said that the pivotal event in the case occurred on Oct. 1 when the city proposed a plan to Time Warner that the city would give up a cable channel designated for public, educational and governmental use, known as PEG, if Time Warner would place the new Fox News program on one of its commercial cable channels. Time Warner refused to "swap" channels with the city to accommodate Fox News, Cote wrote.

"Unwilling to accept Time Warner's decision, a decision protected by the First Amendment and a federal statute, the City raised the ante over the ensuing days in an effort to convince Time Warner to change its mind," Cote wrote.
She said the campaign culminated on Oct. 10, when the city placed Bloomberg Information Television on one of its PEG channels and prepared to place Fox News on another PEG channel.

"I find that by engaging in an effort to compel Time Warner to alter its constitutionally-protected editorial decision not to carry Fox News, the City has violated Time Warner's First Amendment rights," Cote wrote.

The city had argued that it had not tried to interfere with Time Warner's editorial control, but had acted to expand the "diversity of voices" contributing to news, information and public affairs programming. It also said its proposal was aimed at providing more jobs in the New York area.
Cote said that the city's arguments were "entirely unconvincing."
Instead she said that a "substantial and motivating" factor in the city's plan to put Fox and Bloomberg on Crosswalks was to compel Time Warner to run Fox on a commercial channel.

"The conclusion is inescapable that the city's intonation of the rubric 'diversity' is a thinly disguised reference to its preference for the editorial content of Fox News. As such, this rationale for the City's actions cannot constitute a permissable purpose for its actions," Cote wrote.
New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani is scheduled to hold a news conference at noon to discuss the ruling.
Neither News Corp. nor Time Warner had an immediate comment.
